newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: British artist speaks out for Holocaust memorial.
newsitem.headline: British artist speaks out for Holocaust memorial.

text.p: Rachel Whiteread, the British sculptor caught up in a bitter Austrian row, said on Tuesday she hoped her memorial to Vienna Jews killed in the Holocaust would overcome objections and finally see the light of day.

The memorial, brainchild of veteran Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal and funded by the city of Vienna, should have been unveiled on November 9 -- the anniversary of 1938's Crystal Night when Adolf Hitler's Nazis smashed and looted Jewish shops and synagogues across Austria and Germany.
Judenplatz or Jews' Square, the heart of Vienna's thriving mediaeval Jewish community, was the chosen site for the simple, white concrete cast of a library turned in on itself.
But instead of gracing the small baroque square, Whiteread's work is languishing in a workshop outside Vienna while local politicians and the Jewish community squabble.
"I want to see the monument built...in Judenplatz," Whiteread, 33 and winner of the 1993 Turner Prize, told Reuters in an interview.
The square's residents have objected to the scale of the "The Nameless Library" and lamented the loss of parking places.

They have won surprising backing from some Jewish leaders, including Welcome group head Leon Zelman, who argue that the remains of an ancient synagogue beneath the square are eloquent enough. The ruins bear testimony to a pogrom that claimed the lives of hundreds of the city's Jews in 1421.

"I considered the excavations very carefully...but the issue is about something far more contemporary. My brief was to develop a memorial for the 65,000 lost Jews of Vienna," said Whiteread, who normally shuns media attention.

She balks at suggestions that the Holocaust memorial, the first in Vienna to be dedicated solely to the Jewish dead, should be moved to another site. "I thought about space and form...the sculpture should be simple, I hope poetic and dignified."
A jury, including Wiesenthal, selected Whiteread's design in January, saying it symbolised Judaism's survival of persecution through books and writing.
"We are a people of books. Our monuments were never made of stone and steel," Wiesenthal said then.
Assurances from Vienna Mayor Michael Haeupl that the memorial's construction is an "unshakeable fact" have done little to ease Whiteread's growing frustration.
"I thought the City of Vienna would have planned this. I thought the ground had been laid here and people knew what was going on," she said.

Ballooning costs associated with the recovery of the synagogue and plans to build a museum beneath the square have provided ammunition for Whiteread's opponents on the city council. The far-right Freedom Party, the second political force in Vienna, has come out in favour of preserving the synagogue as a memorial.

Nevertheless, Whiteread says she has no regrets about getting involved in the project. "One can never know how something like this would develop. I have had to deal with controversy in the past," she said.

Austria, annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938, has often drawn criticism for its apparent reluctance to shoulder responsibility for the crimes of World War Two. A Vienna monument against "fascism and war" sparked fierce resistance and was only finished in 1991 -- three years behind schedule.
